---
title: "The last app is yours"
---

Every exercise in this book so far told you what to build. This one hands you a
folder called `projects/final-project` and two to three weeks. What the app
does is your decision, and writing that decision down is the first thing you
do.

## Four ways to start {#sec-final-project-directions}

Three directions, and then your own idea. Read all four before you pick,
because the chapters named inside each one are the proof that you can already
build that app.

**A game on an SVG stage.** Something moves on screen, and something in the
rules has an order that matters. The beehive in @sec-beehive-exercise gave you
a grid, a sprite, and arrow keys. The bouncing balls in
@sec-inheritance-exercise gave you a family of things that behave differently
through one abstract base class. Your version adds a structure the rules
actually need, such as a queue of enemies waiting to enter or a stack of moves
the player can take back.

**A drawing tool.** Paint in @sec-callbacks-maps-exercise is the starting
point rather than the target: shapes as classes, a tool selection, an SVG
canvas underneath. Give it multi-level undo with the command pattern from
@sec-undo-command, sitting on the stack you wrote by hand in
@sec-stacks-exercise, and you have a tool people can use badly and recover
from.

**A visualization somebody feeds.** A form takes readings, a chart redraws.
Both halves are already yours, the validating form from @sec-forms-exercise and
the scaling from @sec-charts-scale, so the design work sits in the structure
between them. A queue that holds the last 20 readings and drops the oldest is a
different app from a linked list you insert into in sorted order.

**Your own idea.** Three sentences to your teacher. What the app does, which
classes it needs and which of them is abstract, and which data structure holds
its data and why. If those three sentences hold up, build it.

Whichever way you go, you are building something new. Paint with undo is a new
app; Paint copied into a fresh folder is last term's homework.

## What the project must contain {#sec-final-project-requirements}

Six things, each with a chapter behind it. Read the list before you write your
pitch, because the first two decide what your classes look like.

1. **A class hierarchy with at least one abstract class.** A base class nobody
   can create on its own, with at least two classes extending it. At least one
   of its members is abstract, and every subclass fills that one in differently
   (@sec-inheritance-abstract). Somewhere in your code a variable typed as the
   base class calls that member without asking which kind it is holding. One
   class per file, the way it has been since @sec-polymorphism-modules.

2. **One data structure you wrote yourself.** A linked list, a stack, or a
   queue, with your own `Node<T>` and no array hiding inside it. It has to
   carry data the app really needs, and you have to be able to answer the two
   questions from @sec-choosing-questions about your choice. An array with a
   new name does not count.

3. **Unit tests for the logic.** The rules of your app live in files that never
   mention `document` (@sec-why-test-node), and Vitest tests them. Every rule
   that can be broken gets a test, including the ones that are supposed to
   refuse, such as an empty name or a move the rules forbid.

4. **At least two end-to-end tests.** In `e2e/`, with locators built on roles
   and labels (@sec-playwright-locators). One drives the happy path from an
   empty page to a result on screen. The other drives something that goes
   wrong and checks that the message the user sees is the right one.

5. **An `AGENTS.md` and one skill of your own.** The house rules for this
   project (@sec-skills-agents-md), plus at least one
   `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` that you wrote and actually used
   (@sec-skills-exercise). Anything your buddy got wrong along the way belongs
   in `AGENTS.md` by the time you hand in.

6. **A clean repository with a green check mark.** The app sits in
   `projects/final-project` (@sec-git-course-repo), it has the `verify` script
   in `package.json`, and `.github/workflows/verify.yml` has a job for it that
   runs the unit tests and the end-to-end tests (@sec-verify-ci-workflow,
   @sec-testing-apps-ci). A `README.md` says what the app does and how to start
   it.

## What happens in which week {#sec-final-project-weeks}

**Week one: decide, then stand something up.** Write the pitch and draw the
class diagram (@sec-class-diagrams-mermaid) before you type. Create a new app
from our tests template inside `projects/`, in a folder called `final-project`.
Put the HTML and CSS of the real screen in place even while nothing is behind
it, and copy your data structure and its test file in on day one, so `npm test`
is green before the app does anything.

**Week two: the rules, then the wiring.** Write your classes test first, in the
rhythm every structure in Part 7 was built in. Once the logic is green, wire
`src/index.ts` and watch the app work for the first time. Write your first
end-to-end test that same day, while you still remember which click leads where.

**Week three: finish it.** The second end-to-end test, the error states,
`AGENTS.md`, your skill, the README, and the CI job. If your course gives you
only two weeks, this week has to fit inside the second one, and what you cut is
scope. The tests and the repository are what you are graded on.

**Commit like it matters.** Run `npm run verify` before every commit, make one
commit per thing that works, and push at the end of every session. A history
with a readable message per feature shows your teacher how you worked. A single
commit called "final" shows them nothing, and it also means a broken laptop
costs you the whole project.

**Your buddy, one last time.** The Part 8 buddy holds nothing back. Every
construct in this book is fair game for it now, so it will hand you generics
and Playwright tests without warning you first. That makes the two rules from
@sec-buddy-what heavier rather than lighter. You must be able to explain every
line, and its mistakes are yours. Use it to get unstuck and to speed up work
you already understand, and keep practicing without it, because the exam
happens without it.

## How the project is graded {#sec-final-project-rubric}

Two steps, the way the exams in this course work. The first list decides
whether the project passes at all. The second decides the grade.

### The minimum

Miss any one of these and the project does not pass:

* `npm start` runs the app, and the app does what your pitch said it would.
* At least one abstract class with two classes extending it, and the abstract
  member implemented in both.
* One hand-written data structure that the app really uses.
* `npm test` runs, and at least one test of your own logic is green.
* The project is in `projects/final-project` and pushed to your course
  repository.

### What decides the grade

The minimum is a pass and nothing beyond it. Two things move the grade from
there.

**Completeness.** Everything in @sec-final-project-requirements is present and
working. Both end-to-end tests green, the error states caught and shown to the
user in the page rather than in the console, the CI run green, `AGENTS.md`,
your skill, and the README.

**Code quality.** Logic split from the DOM, one class per file, fields
`private` unless somebody outside genuinely needs them, names that say what the
thing is, `npm run verify` quiet, and tests that read like sentences.
Inheritance and abstraction because the app needed them, and a generic where a
second type would otherwise mean a second copy of the class.

## Shipping the project {#sec-final-project-ship}

Handing in is its own short procedure, and you ran most of it once already in
@sec-toolchain-assets-exercise.

1. Run `npm run verify` until it is quiet.
2. Run `npm run test:e2e` until every test passes.
3. Run `npm run build`, then `npm run preview`, and click through the built app
   at `http://localhost:4173/`. Fix the last thing you find there.
4. Commit, push, open the Actions tab of your repository, and wait for the
   green check mark.
5. Hand in the repository link the way your teacher asks for it.

`npm run preview` and Playwright's own server both want port 4173, so stop the
preview before you run the end-to-end tests again. Playwright says so plainly
when you forget:

```text
Error: http://127.0.0.1:4173 is already used, make sure that nothing is running on the port/url or set reuseExistingServer:true in config.webServer.
```

A year ago you added your own name to a heading in `src/index.ts` and could not
have explained one line of the file it lived in. The app in
`projects/final-project` has classes you designed, a chain of nodes you could
draw from memory, tests that catch you when you break your own rules, and a
browser on a computer in a data center clicking through it after every push.
Nobody wrote the specification for that one. Send the link to somebody and
watch them use it.
